[Why this week matters]{.kicker}

## Even if you never run a simulation

You still need to read performance claims with care.

- what performance claims are built from
- why some model outputs are more trustworthy than others
- where BIM/BEM workflows break in practice

::: {.concept-card}
A simulation number is only as good as the assumptions and cleanup behind it.
:::

---

[The core distinction]{.kicker}

## What are BIM and BEM?

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.concept-card}
[BIM]{.card-title}

- digital model of physical and functional building characteristics
- serves design, construction, coordination, and facility management
- prioritizes geometry, materials, relationships, and documentation
:::

::: {.concept-card}
[BEM]{.card-title}

- computational model of thermal behavior and energy flows
- serves analysis, optimization, and compliance
- prioritizes zones, schedules, systems, weather, and performance assumptions
:::
::::

---

## Same building, different core questions

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.concept-card}
[BIM asks]{.card-title}
What do we build, where does it go, and how is it put together?
:::

::: {.concept-card}
[BEM asks]{.card-title}
How will it behave over time when weather, people, and systems act on it?
:::
::::

---

## Same building, two models

::: {.tool-panel}
::: {.zone .input}
**BIM view** walls · rooms · floors · doors · material layers · element relationships
:::
::: {.zone .operation}
**BEM view** thermal zones · heat-transfer surfaces · schedules · weather · HVAC systems
:::
::: {.zone .output}
**Shared object** the same wall exists in both — but not for the same reason
:::
::: {.zone .check}
**Quality check** does each model carry what its analysis actually needs?
:::
:::

::: {.warning-card}
[Commonly fails to translate]{.card-title}
Thermal **zoning**, occupancy and system **schedules**, real **constructions** (R-value, SHGC, mass), and building **orientation**.
:::

---

[Minimum supported input]{.kicker}

## BIM-derived input schema

For this course, the reliable minimum is not "import my whole model." It is a small table students can export, measure, or enter from Rhino/Revit.

| Field | Unit / type | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| room depth | m | daylight penetration and cooling-load proxy |
| facade orientation | N/E/S/W or degrees | solar exposure and glare risk |
| window-to-wall ratio | 0-1 | daylight gain and heat gain |
| shading depth | m | solar control and view/daylight trade-off |
| glazing U-value / SHGC | numeric | envelope performance assumption |
| obstruction factor | 0-1 | context/shading simplification |

::: {.warning-card}
If this table cannot be filled honestly, a more advanced simulation will only hide the uncertainty better.
:::

---

## BIM data priorities

- project, site, building, levels
- spaces and rooms
- walls, windows, floors, roofs, doors
- material layers and product attributes
- element relationships and construction logic

---

## BEM data priorities

- thermal zones
- heat-transfer surfaces
- internal loads
- occupancy schedules
- HVAC systems and control logic
- weather and shading context

---

[Runnable proxy]{.kicker}

## The performance demo is a scenario file

The minimum runnable route uses a small `scenario.json` or table before any full EnergyPlus/Radiance setup.

::: {.tool-panel}
::: {.zone .input}
**Input** room/facade schema + weather/season assumption
:::
::: {.zone .operation}
**What varies** WWR, shading depth, orientation, glazing, schedule
:::
::: {.zone .output}
**Output** daylight proxy, heat-risk proxy, comfort-risk note
:::
::: {.zone .check}
**Quality check** units, range, and one known hand-check are stated
:::
:::

This proxy is not the final truth. It is the fast test that tells you whether a full Ladybug/Honeybee/Radiance workflow is worth the setup.

## Quick check: BIM or BEM?

1. Exact window manufacturer and product code
2. Occupancy schedule by hour
3. Thermal resistance of an assembly
4. Construction sequencing
5. Cooling setpoint and operating hours

::: {.activity-card}
[Pair task]{.card-title}
Label each item `BIM`, `BEM`, or `both`.
:::

---

## Quick check answers

- exact manufacturer and product code: mostly `BIM`
- occupancy schedule by hour: `BEM`
- thermal resistance of an assembly: often `both`, but used differently
- construction sequencing: `BIM`
- cooling setpoint and operation hours: `BEM`

::: {.concept-card}
The same wall can exist in both models, but not for the same reason.
:::

---

[How the files come to exist]{.kicker}

## How BIM files get made

- **manual BIM authoring** in Revit / ArchiCAD / similar
- **3D import** from Rhino, SketchUp, or other geometric models
- **point cloud capture** for as-built conditions and renovation work

Each path changes how much cleanup is needed before any energy analysis begins.

---

## How BEM files get made

- translate from an existing BIM model
- build a direct energy model from drawings and assumptions
- start from a template or archetype and adapt it

All three approaches are common. None is frictionless.

---

## Workflow map — design to analysis

```{mermaid}
graph TB
    A[Design Intent] --> B[BIM Authoring Tool]
    B --> C[Native BIM File]
    C --> D{Export Format}
    D --> E[IFC]
    D --> F[gbXML]
    F --> G[Energy Modeling Tool]
    G --> H[Initial BEM]
    H --> I[Manual Cleanup]
    I --> J[Schedules, Systems, Controls, Weather]
    J --> K[Complete BEM]
    K --> L[Simulation Results]
```

---

[The translation gap]{.kicker}

## When BIM becomes BEM

Problems usually come from four categories:

- geometry
- zoning
- constructions
- operations

::: {.concept-card}
Translation loss is normal, not an edge case. The skill is anticipating it.
:::

---

## Geometry issues

::: {.warning-card}
- curved facades oversimplified into straight planes
- tiny modeled objects exported as meaningful surfaces
- orientation or context errors
- missing adjacent buildings and shading
:::

---

## Thermal zoning issues

::: {.warning-card}
- BIM spaces do not map neatly to thermal zones
- open offices become fragmented or over-zoned
- plenums, circulation zones, or mixed-use spaces disappear or split badly
:::

---

## Construction and material gaps

::: {.warning-card}
- walls export as generic "exterior wall"
- layers, R-values, SHGC, and internal mass are incomplete
- thermal bridges and details are ignored
:::

---

## Operational data missing

::: {.warning-card}
- no occupancy schedules
- no equipment or lighting schedules
- no setpoints or control strategies
- no HVAC system definitions
:::

This is why a clean-looking import can still be analytically useless.

---

[Translation diagnosis]{.kicker}

## Read the broken translation

::: {.activity-card}
[Scenario]{.card-title}
You exported a 5-story office building to `gbXML` and the first model run shows energy use at **3x** what you expected.
:::

In small groups, work through:

1. What probably happened to the thermal zones?
2. What is likely wrong with the HVAC assumptions?
3. What data probably failed to translate?
4. What would you inspect first before trusting any output?

---

[The two bridges]{.kicker}

## IFC vs `gbXML`

Both are bridges. Neither is a perfect bridge.

| Feature | IFC | `gbXML` |
|---|---|---|
| Primary purpose | broad BIM exchange | energy model translation |
| Geometry detail | high | moderate |
| Thermal zoning support | weak | better |
| File size / speed | heavier | lighter |
| Construction detail | stronger | narrower |

---

## What each bridge is good at

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.concept-card}
[IFC]{.card-title}

- archiving and coordination
- multi-disciplinary interoperability
- detailed building information
:::

::: {.concept-card}
[`gbXML`]{.card-title}

- getting geometry and basic constructions into energy tools
- faster processing
- better starting point for thermal-zone workflows
:::
::::

---

## Why neither solves the whole problem

::: {.warning-card}
- manual cleanup is still required
- vendor implementations vary
- updates overwrite hand fixes
- building design logic and energy logic are not the same thing
:::

---

## Ideal workflow vs real workflow

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.example-card}
[Ideal]{.card-title}

1. update BIM
2. export cleanly
3. update BEM automatically
4. rerun analysis
5. feed changes back into design
:::

::: {.warning-card}
[Real]{.card-title}

1. export once
2. spend days cleaning the BEM
3. design changes continue
4. model diverges
5. everyone hopes the gap is still "small enough"
:::
::::

[A real case]{.kicker}

## Case study: translation gone wrong

- new 15,000 m² university research building
- BIM in Revit with MEP coordination
- energy model in OpenStudio / EnergyPlus
- goal: LEED Gold energy analysis

---

## Case study timeline

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.example-card}
[Week 1]{.card-title}

- export appears successful
- team believes the workflow is seamless
:::

::: {.warning-card}
[Week 2]{.card-title}

- 465 thermal zones created instead of about 30
- HVAC missing
- generic constructions everywhere
- orientation wrong
:::
::::

---

## Case study timeline (cont'd)

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.activity-card}
[Weeks 3-4]{.card-title}

- merge zones manually
- define constructions and material properties
- build schedules and HVAC systems
- fix context and shading
:::

::: {.warning-card}
[Week 8]{.card-title}

- design changes arrive
- re-export means losing cleanup work
- manual updates begin and divergence starts
:::
::::

---

## Lessons learned

::: {.reflection-card}
- BIM was not authored with energy analysis in mind
- missing data only became obvious after export
- there was no workflow for iterative updates
- "the file opened" did not mean "the model is valid"
:::

---

[Translation diagnosis]{.kicker}

## Diagnose the divergence

::: {.activity-card}
[Scenario]{.card-title}
Actual energy use is 30% higher than predicted because the BIM and BEM drifted apart.
:::

In small groups, investigate:

- what geometry changes could explain the increase?
- what material substitutions matter?
- what system or control changes matter?
- what operation schedules may differ from assumptions?

Come back with your top three suspects.

---

## Shared literacy takeaways

::: {.reflection-card}
- BIM and BEM must stay related, but they should not be confused
- simulation outputs are only as good as the assumptions and cleanup behind them
- translation loss is normal, not an edge case
- performance claims need method transparency, not just metrics
:::

---

[Anecdote · clean model, different building]{.kicker}

## The performance gap: models vs metered reality

::: {.warning-card}
[What happens]{.card-title}
Studies of completed buildings repeatedly find measured energy use **two to three times higher** than the design-stage model predicted. The model was not "wrong" — its assumptions (occupancy, schedules, controls, construction quality) simply did not match how the building was actually used and built.
:::

::: {.example-card}
[The lesson]{.card-title}
A polished BEM output is a scenario, not a measurement. State the assumptions a performance claim depends on, and name where the real building is likely to diverge.
:::

[Patch to Grasshopper]{.kicker}

## Performance outputs can steer GH variants

::: {.gh-bridge}
**Bridge pattern**
Use GH/Ladybug/Honeybee or a Python proxy to generate variant metrics -> export `variant_metrics.csv` -> attach daylight/heat-risk scores to GH geometry variants.
:::

::: {.bridge-flow}
::: {.node .current}
BIM-derived schema
:::
::: {.node}
scenario run
:::
::: {.node}
metrics CSV
:::
::: {.node}
GH variant colors
:::
::: {.node}
revise facade
:::
:::

Supported professional bridge: one constrained Ladybug/Radiance walkthrough, not "everything Ladybug."

---

[Uncertainty check]{.kicker}

## Simulation is precise about the model, not automatically about the building

::: {.uncertainty-check}
**Question for your performance route**
Which assumption dominates the result: geometry, material, schedule, weather, system, or occupancy?
:::

If you cannot name the dominant assumption, do not present the output as a performance conclusion. Present it as a scenario result.

## Reconstruct your model in four steps

**Object this week: your BIM/BEM model and one performance claim.**

::: {.recall-4step}
::: {.step}
**Did** What does the model claim, and what did you actually build or export?
:::
::: {.step}
**Assumed** What zoning, schedules, and constructions did the workflow assume for you?
:::
::: {.step}
**Risk** Where could the translation have failed without you noticing?
:::
::: {.step}
**Verify** What would you inspect before trusting the output?
:::
:::

::: {.grading-note}
Post your filled four-step to Slack under your material. Posting + an honest reconstruction is the graded unit — not how you spoke. Presenting is welcomed and earns credit; it is never required and never scored as performance.
:::
